title: India's food prices set to rise further as El Niño weakens monsoon, economists warn
excerpt: With August retail inflation at a 20-month high of 4.82% and the monsoon deficit the worst since FY16, economists warn food-price pressures could keep inflation above 5% and force the RBI's hand.
body:
• India's retail inflation climbed to 4.82% in August — a 20-month high — driven by food and fuel prices, with the data released on September 14.
  • An erratic monsoon, record sugar prices and crude oil near $100 a barrel pushed up essentials from cereals and milk to edible oils and meat.
  • Food inflation has run at around 8% year-on-year since November 2023; export curbs and tariff cuts have had little effect.
  • Economists warn food-price pressures will keep inflation above 5% in the second half of the fiscal year, strengthening the case for an RBI rate hike as early as October.

India's food prices are likely to rise further and stay elevated, economists say, as a weak monsoon, strengthening El Niño conditions and rising global energy costs combine to keep pressure on household budgets — with August retail inflation printing at 4.82%, a 20-month high, according to Reuters.

Context & Background

Annual consumer price inflation rose to 4.82% in August from 4.45% in July, marking a third straight month above the Reserve Bank of India's 4% medium-term target. Food, which accounts for nearly half of the consumer price basket, did the heavy lifting: an erratic monsoon disrupted supplies of sugar, cereals, milk, edible oils, eggs and meat. Sugar prices hit a record high in August, adding at least 15 basis points to headline inflation, according to Kanika Pasricha, chief economic adviser at Union Bank of India. Crude oil nearing $100 a barrel and higher cooking gas prices added fuel pressure, while core inflation — excluding food and fuel — was estimated at 4.1%.

This is not a new flare-up. Food inflation has remained around 8% year-on-year since November 2023, driven by supply-side shocks, Reuters reported in an explainer. Last year's drought and an ongoing heat wave cut supplies of pulses, vegetables and cereals. Temperatures in nearly half the country have soared 4-9 degrees Celsius above normal, spoiling harvested and stored vegetables and hindering the planting of onions, tomatoes, eggplant and spinach. Export curbs and reduced import tariffs have had little effect.

"The increase is expected to be primarily driven by elevated food prices together with a further rise in fuel inflation."

— Kanika Pasricha, Chief Economic Adviser, Union Bank of India

Impact & Analysis

The forward-looking risks sit with the monsoon. India's current monsoon deficit is the highest since fiscal year 2016, driven by strengthening El Niño conditions, Gaura Sen Gupta, economist at IDFC First Bank, told Mint. Reservoir levels are running below their 10-year average and uneven spatial distribution threatens both kharif and rabi crops. Kharif sowing remains marginally below last year's levels, with rice sowing tracking lower. Although irrigation coverage has improved to 60%, substantial sowing still depends on monsoon performance, and El Niño is expected to peak in November-December.

Sen Gupta's assessment splits the risk: adequate food grain stocks mitigate some inflation risk for cereals, but perishables — which cannot be stored — remain the challenge. The weakness could also stress rural demand post-harvest in the March quarter, dampening rural consumption. Economists see inflation staying above 5% in the second half of the fiscal year. Radhika Rao of DBS Bank noted food inflation continues to rise on pulses, sugar and dairy, with energy prices volatile and input costs gradually filtering through to consumers. Oxford Economics' Alexandra Hermann Prasad expects inflation to move above 5% in coming months and breach the RBI's 6% upper tolerance limit in the October-December quarter, with "second round pressures building".

Policy room is narrow. With inflation inside the 2-6% band, the RBI held rates at its last meeting, though minutes signalled readiness to tighten if price pressures broadened. Rate rises are not expected before next year by the poll consensus — but analysts now say the case for an October hike is strengthening.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the numbers matter two ways: families in India face higher grocery bills and softening rural demand, while non-resident investors watch RBI policy — a rate hike would move the rupee and Indian debt markets. Food inflation has also been the single biggest factor keeping the central bank from cutting rates.

What's Next

September rainfall will decide the rabi outlook, with reservoir levels the number to watch. If El Niño peaks as expected in November-December, food-price pressures could persist into early next year — keeping inflation above the RBI's comfort zone and the rate-hike debate alive.
